references.text: Overall, 215,504 assets constituting 94.1%, were classified as functional and in use, while 13,520 (5.9%) were classified as faulty and out of use. The detailed analysis of asset condition is indicated in table 1.

As indicated in table 1 above, most of the deployed assets were already in service while some were in store and still in good condition but not in use. This was attributed mainly to some localized challenges such as power, incomplete structures, untrained staff, among others. Some assets were broken mainly furniture in Seed Secondary Schools and require repair.
Figure 2 shows the reasons for non-deployment of some of the assets even when they were found to be in good condition.

Identification varied at the different asset locations. Identifiers are recorded for 30.3% of MDA records, 24.5% of school records and 15.0% of health-centre records. Of the 193 seed schools, 144 (74.6%) reported at least one benefit. A better learning environment, with classrooms, furniture and libraries, was reported by 74 (38.3%), and improved access to secondary education or shorter distances by 59 (30.6%). Frequency. Few facilities worked to a fixed maintenance interval. Of the 494 programme-list facilities that described how they maintain UgIFT assets or check their condition, 50 (10.1%) did so at a fixed interval. Of these 50, 14 (28.0%) worked annually, 11 (22.0%) monthly, 10 (20.0%) quarterly, 9 (18.0%) every school term, 3 (6.0%) twice a year and 3 (6.0%) weekly or daily, as Figure 47 shows. protected_paragraph_format_matches.text: 1 Introduction and background
1.1 Introduction

This report presents the findings of the UgIFT asset verification undertaken by the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development as part of programme closure activities. It sets out the status of the assets provided by the programme to the targeted national institutions responsible for supporting the implementation of the programme, Blood Banks and local governments specifically targeting Seed Secondary Schools and health facilities upgraded from Health Centre II to Health Centre III.
1.2 Background to the verification

The Uganda Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (UgIFT) Programme is a government programme implemented through a Programme-for-Results (PforR) launched and aligned with the broader IGFT Reform Programme (2015). UgIFT 1.0 began with US$200 million in FY2017/18, supporting Education and Health. This was later expanded through additional financing of US$300 million, including US$240 million in credit and US$60 million in grants, with US$50 million from the IDA Refugee Support Window, expanding beyond Education and Health to water and Environment and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation) making the overall funding total of US$500 million.

The Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfer Reform Programme (IGFT RP) was revised in 2020 to align with the Third National Development Plan (NDP III 2020/21 - 2024/25), and to directly contribute to Four (04) Programmes i.e. Human Capital Development; Public Sector Transformation; Natural Resources, Environment, Climate change, Land and Water Management; and Development Plan Implementation.

Overall, the development objective of the UgIFT Programme was to: “Improve the adequacy, equity, and effectiveness of financing and the oversight, management, and delivery of Local Government services in Education, Health, Water and Environment, and Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation), including refugees and their host communities”.
Specifically, the Programme sought to:
Increase the adequacy and predictability of fiscal transfers to Local Governments for service delivery;
Improve the equity and transparency of allocation mechanisms through the introduction of formula-based transfers;
Strengthen performance incentives and accountability systems for Local Governments; and
Expand access to quality education and health infrastructure, particularly in under-served areas.
The UgIFT Programme had four components aimed at strengthening the intergovernmental fiscal transfer system while supporting investments in service delivery infrastructure. These included;
Component 1: Reform of the Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfer System

This supported the design and implementation of a reformed fiscal transfer framework based on objective and transparent allocation criteria. This resulted into introduction of formula-based grants - Revised allocation formulas reflecting population, infrastructure gaps, and service delivery needs.
Component 2: Education Infrastructure Development

This component financed the construction and upgrading of education facilities, particularly government secondary schools in under-served sub-counties. This involved construction and equipping of new secondary schools - classrooms, laboratories, administration blocks, sanitation facilities, teachers’ houses, furniture and ICT equipment in the different local governments.
Component 3: Health Infrastructure Development

This supported investments in health facilities to improve access to primary health care services at the local level. The major outputs under the component were construction and upgrading of health centers - Staff accommodation, sanitation facilities and provision of medical equipment.
Component 4: Local Government Performance and Institutional Strengthening

This aimed at strengthening LG capacity in planning, budgeting, procurement, and infrastructure management. Under this component, annual Local Government Performance Assessments have been undertaken across the 176 LGs, capacity building and technical support strengthened monitoring and reporting systems.

The Programme was implemented through a clearly defined results framework that connected actions and incentives across three levels of government to strengthen service delivery outcomes. The programme came to an end on 31 December 2025. The following areas of support describe the following outputs under the different components; current asset and facility findings are presented later in this report.
Budget Support
Education: 196 of 259 Seed Secondary Schools are complete of which 189 are operational.
Health: 354 of 373 health facilities, upgrades/new constructions (HC II to HC III) are complete.

Water and Environment: 758 - piped water systems, 5,398- point water sources, 7,082 water supply systems rehabilitated, 325 designs completed, and 256 sanitation facilities in the targeted service units.
Agriculture (Micro-scale Irrigation): Over 6,235 irrigation systems were installed (4,843 hectares under irrigation), 632 irrigation demonstration sites in 135 LGs set up.
Refugee intervention: 51 primary schools and 35 health facilities in refugee hosting districts (RHD) were transitioned and integrated into the LG service.
Blood Banks: Regional Blood Banks in Arua and Hoima were completed and commissioned while Soroti Regional Blood Bank was rehabilitated.
2.Grant management

Assets for institutional strengthening and retooling including ICT equipment and vehicles were provided. The Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) through PFM Coordination Unit (RCU) manages the Government of Uganda counterpart funding of the programme to support the grant management component of the UgIFT programme. The grant management supports in financing of Central Government actions intended to achieve programme objectives and Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLIs). To this end, MoFPED through RCU supported MDAs to acquire different assets meant to support programme implementation.
1.3 Justification

The UgIFT programme came to an end on 31st December 2025. As part of the programme’s closure activities, MoFPED, through RCU, commissioned an end-of-programme asset verification exercise to take stock of the assets procured under the programme and to establish where those assets were, how they were being used as part of the processes to hand them over to government for sustainability purposes.
1.4 Objectives of the assignment
The objective of the assignment was to undertake verification and recording of all assets acquired under the UgIFT Programme. Specifically, the assignment intended to;
Identify and verify the existence of the assets
Verify the assets condition and status: specifically, the condition on functionality, usage/performance and location among others
Assess financial management aspects: residual value of the investments/hardware/tools for purposes of financial reporting for project closure
List the assets that are obsolete, unserviceable and require disposal
Develop a computerized database of the investment/hardware/tools to facilitate recording of new deployed assets/investments.
Undertake PFM Assessment on Asset Management practices (including sustainability, Operations and Maintenance) of the UgIFT implementing LGs
1.5 Scope of Work

The assignment covered institutions at national and local government level that directly implemented the UgIFT programme through coordination, support and implementation. At local government level, the study focused on upgraded health facilities and Seed Secondary Schools that received assets under the programme. Health Centers and other local-government assets are also reported separately.
Specifically, the assignment involved the following tasks;
Verification of the Asset’s Records of targeted ministries departments and agencies and local governments
Physical and Functional Verification of assets
Data Consolidation for generation of a single data base of assets provided by the program
Generation of an IFMIS ready Asset Register for Integration, and Migration into IFMIS
Review of the UgIFT Asset Management Practices
1.6 Expected deliverables
Key expected outputs of the consultant include:
Report with the list and current status of assets acquired under the programmes;
An automated up-to-date assets data base of UgIFT Investments across MDALGs;
Report on the estimated value of assets under the programme as well as operations and maintenance arrangements;
IFMIS-Ready Asset Register and Data Migration Report
Report on functionality of assets relating to systems investments;
Report on Assessment of Asset Management Practices, Risks and recommendations.
2 Approach and methodology

The verification exercise was conducted using a participatory and consultative process and implemented in three interlinked phases: Preparatory and inception phase, Data collection phase and the report writing phase.
2.1 Preparation

After signing of the contract, the assignment commenced with an entry meeting on 28th May 2026. During this meeting, the Client specified target MDAs to be visited, the LG stakeholders to be reached as well as the documents to be reviewed. The Inception phase was completed and the inception report submitted on 18th June, 2026 which provided an agreed scope, approach and work plan for the exercise.
2.2 Pilot Test

The team also undertook a pilot test in Wakiso District Local Government, with verification carried out at Buloba Health Centre III and Sumbwe Seed Secondary School. During the pilot test, it was found out that, among others, there are cases of mismatches of facility names, that UgIFT assets can be integrated into the general LG asset register. This facilitated improving the design of the data collection process including; design of data collection tools, determining the timeline for data collection and estimated costs.
2.3 Data collection
This exercise was undertaken in two phases first at National level and later at the Local government level.

National level: Physical visits to verify assets provided by the programme at the national-level was completed on the 19th of August 2026. This covered 15 MDAs including; Ministry of Works and Transport (MoWT); Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES); Ministry of Agriculture, Animal Industries and Fisheries (MAAIF); Ministry of Health (MoH); Office of the Prime Minister (OPM); Ministry of Water and Environment (MoWE); Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development (MoGLSD); Local Government Finance Commission; National Environment Management Authority (NEMA); Public Procurement and Disposal of Assets Authority (PPDA); Office of the Auditor General (OAG); Ministry of Public Service (MoPs); Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development (MoLHUD); Ministry of Local Government (MoLG) and Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED). Additionally, three Blood Banks of Hoima, Arua and Soroti were covered.

Local government level: The local government verification targeted UgIFT upgraded or constructed Health Centres and Seed Secondary Schools. The programme reconciliation list contains 629 distinct entries: 371 Health Centres and 258 schools under 160 recorded local government names. The process began with training of field teams prior to the actual field verification.

Training of field teams: A total of 85 Research Assistants (RAs) and 7 Regional Supervisors were trained. The training took place from 21st to 23rd August 2026 while physical verification started on the 24th of August 2026. During the asset verification, the RAs visited Seed Secondary Schools, Health Centres and Blood Banks.

Physical verification: This exercise commenced on the 24th of August 2026 and was completed on 17th September 2026. The local government physical verification involved entry meetings with the LG leadership at the LG headquarters for authorization and review of reports relating to UgIFT assets, key informant interviews with the technical teams especially the Chief Administrative Officers, Finance Officers, District Health Officers and District Education Officers. Thereafter, the RAs proceeded to the facilities for physical verification of the assets.

At local government level, the programme list had 629 facilities: 371 Health Centres and 258 Seed Secondary Schools. The list recorded 547 facilities (87.0%) as complete and 82 (13.0%) as ongoing. The ongoing works were more common among Seed Secondary Schools (63, or 24.4%) than among Health Centres (19, or 5.1%).
2.4 Quality assurance

Regional supervisors checked daily field activity and reviewed the completed tools. The central technical team carried out spot checks and helped resolve operational questions. Teams compared institutional asset information with the items and explanations provided during visits, while supervisors referred matters requiring clarification to the team leader and field coordinator.
2.5 Asset categories, condition, use and identification

Asset categories: Each entry in the Asset Register represents one recorded unit. The analysis covers buildings, ICT equipment, transport equipment, furniture and fittings, medical, laboratory and research equipment, other classified assets, items outside fixed-asset classification and unclassified entries. Assets are grouped by the institution or beneficiary to which they are attributed.

Condition and use: Condition and use were reported for each asset during the verification. A working asset is one recorded as functional and in use. An asset recorded as faulty was reported as not working and not in use. This included assets that were broken down or damaged. An asset that was new and in store was recorded as functional but not in use. Additionally, an asset that was held elsewhere, not yet delivered or awaiting power installation, completion of buildings or trained users, was also recorded as functional but not in use.

Identification: An asset is properly identified when carried a UgIFT programme marking. However, there were other assets that had no UgIFT marking but the officers on ground identified them as UgIFT assets.
2.6 Financial analysis and Valuation

The Government of Uganda Asset Accounting Policies and Guidelines 2023 was used to determine as the policy basis for determining recorded values, depreciation and net book values. Financial values are reported as at 30th September 2026. Straight-line depreciation was applied where the required information was available.
2.7 Analysis and reporting

Analysis and reporting was done through triangulation of the literature from different policy, Planning and Financial documents including: Government of Uganda Asset Accounting Policies and Guidelines 2023; asset registers; asset records at national and local government levels; physical inspections; discussions with facility managers; photographs and asset counts for each institution.
2.8 Challenges and Limitations to the assignment

Difficult terrain and poor physical accessibility of facilities: Physical accessibility presented a significant operational challenge especially for facilities located in areas characterised by difficult terrain and limited transport accessibility such as Bwesumbu HC III, Bwesumbu Seed School, Buhuhira and Kabingo in Kasese District. In addition, accessing facilities within the Island was difficult, time consuming and expensive. This led the teams to overshoot the anticipated time for data collection.

High transportation cost: Given the national wide coverage, the rising fuel prices led to high field costs. The field teams spent more money than was anticipated. The costs were extra ordinarily higher for island facilities like Kalangala, Buvuma, Mayuge among others. For instance, Kalangala had 3 facilities with long distance on water that required hiring a private boat since it was not a common route to the transporters and outside the ferry schedules. A similar situation was encountered in Buvuma and Namayingo districts.

Poor record keeping: In many LGs and facilities, there were no clear records about the assets delivered under UgIFT. The LGs and the facilities had incomplete or missing UgIFT asset registers which delayed data collection. Subsequently, the teams took longer in such facilities identifying the assets as most of these were not engraved with the UgIFT identifiers while others were not engraved at all. In addition, the field teams encountered situations where some Assets could not be physically accessed especially for schools since it was holiday time.
3 Findings

This section presents results of the verification exercise based on the specific objectives. The results are presented in different results levels indicating availability of assets, asset condition and functionality, asset marking and identification and the financial analysis in each subsection.
3.1 Overall results
This section provides an overall view of the UgFT asset status combining both National level agencies and schools and health centres.
Overall asset availability

A total of 229,024 assets are recorded across the targeted MDAs, beneficiary Blood Banks, Upgraded Health Centres and Seed Secondary School. These include vehicles, laptops, printers, desktop computers, projectors, cameras, furniture (desks, chairs, tables and stools), UPS systems, digital phones, paper shredders, tablets and clinical equipment, among others.

Overall, the Seed Secondary Schools hold the majority of assets 63.4% (145,256), followed by Health Centres with 27.7% (63,432). MDAs hold 7.3% (16,663) and regional Blood Banks with 0.3% (602). In addition, some assets were found to have been reallocated by LGs from Health Center to hospitals such as Rukoki general hospital in Kasese Municipality.
